title: The First Political Parties, 1796–1800
summary: Compare how each state's electors voted in 1796 and 1800, see which states changed sides, and work out whether one state decided the election of 1800.
subject: History
time: About 57 minutes: 47 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

map.about: This map compares the elections of 1796 and 1800 state by state: a pie on each of the sixteen states shows how its electors voted in the contests between John Adams (Federalist) and Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican). The 1800 layer is off when the map opens, because the two sets of pies overlap. Two pink squares mark landmark Supreme Court cases that tested the new federal government's power: Marbury v. Madison (1803) in Washington, D.C., and McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) in Baltimore. This lesson's questions use the two election layers only.

image.alt: The eastern United States in 1796, each state with a pie of electors' votes in orange and blue (bigger pies for more electors), and two pink squares, one labeled Marbury v. Madison (1803).

compellingQuestion.en: How did the first political parties divide the country?
compellingQuestion.es: ¿Cómo dividieron al país los primeros partidos políticos?

questions.task: Open The sixteen states bookmark. Use the pies and the legend to find which regions mostly voted for Adams and which for Jefferson, and click the two-color pies for the split states' numbers.
frontOfClass: Open The sixteen states bookmark.
Open the legend: orange for John Adams, blue for Thomas Jefferson.
Point out that bigger pies mean more electors.
Ask: which part of the country mostly voted for Adams, and which for Jefferson?
Click one two-color pie and read the 1796 votes line of the pop-up.
Ask: which states split their votes, and how?

steps.es: Abre el marcador The sixteen states (Los dieciséis estados).

steps.en: Use the legend to read the 1796 pies.
steps.es: Usa la leyenda para leer los gráficos circulares de 1796.

steps.en: Click each two-color pie and read its pop-up.
steps.es: Haz clic en cada gráfico de dos colores y lee su ventana emergente.

ask.en: Which part of the country mostly voted for Adams, and which for Jefferson? Which states split their votes, and how?
ask.es: ¿Qué parte del país votó sobre todo por Adams y cuál por Jefferson? ¿Qué estados dividieron sus votos, y cómo?

answer.where: The sixteen states bookmark; Election of 1796: electors' votes layer. Legend: orange = John Adams, blue = Thomas Jefferson; the pop-up names the state. All-orange pies: Connecticut, Delaware, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont. All-blue: Georgia, Kentucky, South Carolina, Tennessee. Two-color pies, from the pop-up's 1796 votes line: Maryland (Adams 7, Jefferson 4), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 14, Adams 1), Virginia (Jefferson 20, Adams 1), North Carolina (Jefferson 11, Adams 1).
answer.accept: Adams: New England and the states around New York (New York, New Jersey, Delaware). Jefferson: the South and the West, plus most of Pennsylvania. The four split states named, with Maryland the only split state Adams won.
answer.text: The totals are not on the map: Adams 71, Jefferson 68, so Jefferson, the runner-up, became vice president.

questions.task: Turn off Election of 1796 and turn on Election of 1800. Find the two-color pies and click each for the numbers; identify the closest state.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn off Election of 1796: electors' votes and turn on Election of 1800: electors' votes.
Ask: which states have two-color pies this time?
Click one of them and read the 1800 votes line of the pop-up.
Ask: how did its electors divide, and which state was the closest?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn off Election of 1796 and turn on Election of 1800.
steps.es: En las capas del mapa (Map layers), desactiva Election of 1796 (Elección de 1796) y activa Election of 1800 (Elección de 1800).
Busca los gráficos de dos colores.

steps.en: Click each one and read how its electors divided.
steps.es: Haz clic en cada uno y lee cómo se dividieron sus electores.

ask.en: Which states have two-color pies this time? How did each one's electors divide between Adams and Jefferson? Which state was the closest?
ask.es: ¿Qué estados tienen gráficos de dos colores esta vez? ¿Cómo se dividieron los electores de cada uno entre Adams y Jefferson? ¿Qué estado estuvo más reñido?

answer.where: Election of 1800: electors' votes layer; two-color pies, pop-up 1800 votes line: Maryland (Jefferson 5, Adams 5), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 8, Adams 7), North Carolina (Jefferson 8, Adams 4). Closest: Maryland, an even split.
answer.text: Totals, not on the map: Jefferson 73, Burr 73, Adams 65. Each elector cast two votes, so the pop-ups also list Burr and Charles C. Pinckney.

questions.task: Compare the two elections by switching between Election of 1796 and Election of 1800 in Map layers. Find the state whose whole pie changed color, the states whose shares changed, and describe where each party was strong.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, switch Election of 1796 off and Election of 1800 on, then back, so the class sees the change.
Ask: which state's whole pie changed from orange to blue?
Click that state's pie and read the number of electors in the pop-up title.
Switch the layers again and look at the two-color pies.
Ask: which states' pies changed their shares, and did any New England state change?
Ask: where was each party strong, and where did the two compete?

steps.en: In Map layers, switch between Election of 1796 and Election of 1800 (one on, one off).
steps.es: En las capas del mapa, alterna entre Election of 1796 y Election of 1800 (una activada, la otra desactivada).

steps.en: Find the state whose whole pie changed from orange to blue, and click it to read its electors.
steps.es: Busca el estado cuyo gráfico entero cambió de naranja a azul y haz clic en él para leer sus electores.

steps.en: Find the states whose pies changed their shares, and check New England.
steps.es: Busca los estados cuyos gráficos cambiaron sus proporciones y fíjate en Nueva Inglaterra.

ask.en: Which state's whole pie changed from orange to blue, and how many electors did it have? Which states' pies changed their shares, and did any New England state change? Using both maps, where was each party strong and where did the two parties compete?
ask.es: ¿Qué estado cambió todo su gráfico de naranja a azul, y cuántos electores tenía? ¿Qué estados cambiaron las proporciones de su gráfico, y cambió algún estado de Nueva Inglaterra? Con los dos mapas, ¿dónde era fuerte cada partido y dónde competían los dos partidos?

answer.where: Election of 1796 and Election of 1800 layers, pop-up title (state and number of electors) and votes lines. New York, 12 electors: all Adams in 1796, all Jefferson in 1800. Shares changed: Maryland (Adams 7–4 to 5–5), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 14–1 to 8–7), North Carolina (Jefferson 11–1 to 8–4), Virginia (Jefferson 20–1 to 21–0). No New England state changed: Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont stayed all orange.
answer.accept: Names New York as the only state that switched entirely; notes that the middle states (Maryland, Pennsylvania, North Carolina) were split in both elections; says the Federalists were strong in New England and the Democratic-Republicans in the South and West, with the middle states (and New York) deciding the result.
answer.text: New York's 12 votes were more than the margin: without that switch Adams would have had 77 votes to Jefferson's 61 in 1800, instead of 65 to 73.

title.en: Did one state decide the election?

questions.task: With Election of 1800 on, students click New York and the split states, read the electors' votes, and work out what the result would have been if New York had voted as it did in 1796.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, make sure Election of 1800 is on and Election of 1796 is off.
Click New York and read its electors in the pop-up title: 12, all for Jefferson.
Give the class the totals, which are not on the map: Jefferson 73, Adams 65.
Ask: if New York's 12 electors had voted for Adams, as in 1796, what would the totals have been?
Click Maryland, Pennsylvania and North Carolina. Ask: which other states were close enough to change the result?

steps.en: In Map layers, make sure Election of 1800 is on.
steps.es: En las capas del mapa (Map layers), comprueba que Election of 1800 esté activada.

steps.en: Click New York and read how many electors it had and how they voted.
steps.es: Haz clic en Nueva York y lee cuántos electores tenía y cómo votaron.

steps.en: Click the two-color pies again and read how close each state was.
steps.es: Vuelve a hacer clic en los gráficos de dos colores y lee qué tan reñido estuvo cada estado.

ask.en: In 1800 Jefferson won 73 electors' votes and Adams 65. If New York had voted as it did in 1796, what would the totals have been? Which other states were close enough to change the result?
ask.es: En 1800 Jefferson obtuvo 73 votos de electores y Adams 65. Si Nueva York hubiera votado como en 1796, ¿cuáles habrían sido los totales? ¿Qué otros estados estuvieron lo bastante reñidos como para cambiar el resultado?

answer.where: Election of 1800: electors' votes layer. New York pop-up title: 12 electors, all for Jefferson in 1800 (all for Adams in 1796). Moving those 12 gives Adams 65 + 12 = 77 and Jefferson 73 − 12 = 61. Split states, from the 1800 votes line: Maryland (Jefferson 5, Adams 5), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 8, Adams 7), North Carolina (Jefferson 8, Adams 4).
answer.accept: Adams 77, Jefferson 61: New York's switch was enough to decide the election. Maryland (5 to 5) and Pennsylvania (8 to 7) were the closest states. A swing of five electors anywhere would also have reversed the result (65 + 5 = 70 against 73 − 5 = 68), so accept either state with that reasoning.
answer.text: The totals are not on the map, so the question gives them. Each elector cast two votes, which is why Jefferson and Burr tied at 73; the pop-ups explain it.

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from both election layers. Accept answers that name a region for each party and use the split states or New York's switch as evidence. A paragraph, or a sketch that marks each party's region (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), both work.

student.en: Answer the big question. Name each party's region, and use one state that split or switched as your evidence.
student.es: Responde la pregunta central. Nombra la región de cada partido y usa como evidencia un estado que se dividió o que cambió de bando.

objectives: Use the pies and legend of the Election of 1796 layer to describe which regions voted mostly for Adams and which for Jefferson, and click the split states for their numbers.
Switch between the 1796 and 1800 layers to find the state whose whole pie changed color and the states whose shares changed.
Read the two-color pies in the Election of 1800 layer to identify the closest state.
Use New York's electors and the split states in the Election of 1800 layer to work out whether one state decided the election.
Use the pattern of electors' votes across the sixteen states as evidence to describe where each party was strong in 1800.
discussion: Comparing the 1796 and 1800 pies, where did the Federalists hold on and where did they lose ground? What do those regions have in common on the map?
In both elections a few states split their electors between the two candidates. Which states were they, and why might a state's electors not all vote the same way?
New York's 12 electors all changed sides between 1796 and 1800. What might make a whole state change its vote in four years, and what would you want to find out to check your idea?

differentiation.support: Do question 1 from the front with the legend open, and write the two candidates and their colors on the board before pairs click the split states.
differentiation.stretch: Click the pink square at Washington, D.C. and read the Marbury v. Madison pop-up. What did the change of party in 1801 have to do with this case?

assessment.evidence: Strong answers use the pies and legend of the Election of 1796 and Election of 1800 layers (orange for Adams, blue for Jefferson) with numbers from the pop-ups, such as New York's 12 electors switching from all Adams to all Jefferson, Maryland 7–4 then 5–5 and Pennsylvania 14–1 then 8–7.
assessment.exemplar: The first parties split the country by region. In 1796 every New England state voted for Adams, the Federalist. Georgia, Kentucky, South Carolina and Tennessee all voted for Jefferson. The states in the middle were divided. Maryland gave Adams 7 votes and Jefferson 4, and four years later it split 5 to 5. Pennsylvania went from 14 to 1 for Jefferson to 8 to 7. The biggest change was New York. All 12 of its electors voted for Adams in 1796 and all 12 voted for Jefferson in 1800. No New England state changed at all. So each party had a region it could count on, and the election was decided in a few states between them.

beforeYouStart.en: George Washington belonged to no party, and in 1796, as he prepared to leave office, he warned Americans against parties. By then two had formed: the Federalists, led by John Adams and Alexander Hamilton, and the Democratic-Republicans, led by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison. Each elector cast two votes for president, and the runner-up became vice president.
beforeYouStart.es: George Washington no pertenecía a ningún partido y, en 1796, cuando se preparaba para dejar la presidencia, advirtió a los estadounidenses contra los partidos. Para entonces ya se habían formado dos: los federalistas, encabezados por John Adams y Alexander Hamilton, y los demócrata-republicanos, encabezados por Thomas Jefferson y James Madison. Cada elector emitía dos votos para presidente, y quien quedaba en segundo lugar era vicepresidente.

readingTheMap.en: The map has no place names: click a pie to see the state's name and its number of electors. Each pie shows how a state's electors voted: orange for John Adams (Federalist) and blue for Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican); use the legend. Bigger pies mean more electors. Each elector cast two votes; the pop-up lists the other candidates. Election of 1800 is off when the map opens. Pink squares mark two Supreme Court cases; this lesson does not use them. Maine is shown within Massachusetts and West Virginia within Virginia, and territories aren't shown.
readingTheMap.es: El mapa no tiene nombres de lugares: haz clic en un gráfico circular para ver el nombre del estado y su número de electores. Cada gráfico muestra cómo votaron los electores de un estado: naranja para John Adams (federalista) y azul para Thomas Jefferson (demócrata-republicano); usa la leyenda. Los gráficos más grandes indican más electores. Cada elector emitía dos votos; la ventana emergente muestra a los demás candidatos. La capa Election of 1800 está desactivada al abrir el mapa. Los cuadrados rosados marcan dos casos de la Corte Suprema; esta lección no los usa. Maine aparece dentro de Massachusetts y Virginia Occidental dentro de Virginia, y no se muestran los territorios.

reflection.en: If you could have changed the result in one state in 1800, which would you pick, and why that one?
reflection.es: Si hubieras podido cambiar el resultado en un solo estado en 1800, ¿cuál elegirías, y por qué ese?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: When the map opens, Election of 1796 and the Supreme Court layer are on and Election of 1800 is off, because the two sets of pie charts overlap. Students switch between the two elections in Map layers for questions 2 and 3.

misconceptions.response: Electors did, and states chose their electors in different ways. In 1796 and 1800 each elector cast two votes.
They were rivals from different parties: in 1796 Jefferson, the runner-up, became Adams's vice president.

misconceptions.claim: The 1800 tie was between Jefferson and Adams.
misconceptions.response: It was between Jefferson and his own running mate, Aaron Burr, with 73 votes each.
